vignette: The night the dock at Waimanalo changed for Tiana began like any other shift in her nets and hauler lines. She was eighteen then, hauling gear alongside her cousin Eli, when a cluster of men arrived on bicycles, their wheels clacking against the wet concrete. One of the riders dismounted, and what followed was a blur of shoved hands, the sharp intake of Eli's breath, and the heavy, frantic footsteps padding across the pier. Tiana had watched him fall, her own hands gripping the rusted frame of her bicycle parked nearby, the chain links catching the dock lights like cold teeth. The sirens that wailed afterward seemed to merge with the metallic screech of the bike gears in her ears, and when the ambulance doors finally closed, she knew nothing about those sounds would ever sit quietly again. In the weeks that followed, Tiana noticed her ribs tightening before she could even name what she was afraid of. When she was waiting for a ferry or for a reply to a message, the silence stretched until she was certain something terrible was unfolding. Her mind would fracture into fragments that arrived without warning, often stripping away any clear picture but leaving the full weight of panic in her chest. When an image did surface, it was always tangled with a sharp, suffocating guilt-she kept circling the thought that she should have pulled Eli out of the way, that her hands had been so close and yet so useless. She took on extra shifts, keeping her hands busy until the salt air and the groan of winches filled the hours. She began leaving her phone face-down during conversations, instead locking herself in her room for hours with games and videos playing on a loop. Raised in her family's Pacific tradition of stoic endurance, she found herself unmoored. Her boyfriend, Julian, noticed the distance creeping in. When he reached for her, when the evening grew quiet and close, she would tense and pull away, convinced that intimacy would only make the walls of her own skin too thin. The harbor itself continued to present specific demands. Riding her bicycle to the work dock at dawn, the rhythmic click of the chain or the sight of a parked wheel sent her pulse skittering up her throat. She circled the lot from the far gate, avoiding the sounds of nearby boats and the echoing footfalls of other workers, telling herself it was just safer that way. Tiana had come to see her own reactions as a betrayal. Her shoulders would jump at a sudden noise, her breath would hitch before her mind could catch up, and she grew certain that her body was still living inside that night, mistaking every shadow for an approaching threat. The thought that she might one day lose control of her temper, that the pressure building behind her ribs would crack open into something unmanageable, kept her pacing the floor long after her shifts ended. The concentration fog settled heavily over her daily tasks, making it hard to read her charts or keep track of the catch. What finally brought her to the clinic was the morning she dropped a crate of halibut. Her hands had gone numb in the middle of a routine haul, and she sat on the dock afterwards, listening to the gulls and the slap of water against the pilings. She admitted that she did not know how to stop feeling like a stranger in her own skin. She came hoping to unclench the constant vigilance that had taken up residence in her chest, afraid that if she didn't learn to trust her own breath again, she would either break completely or break something else in the process.
